prompt:
Below are 8 separate research decisions, each with two options. In each item, one option is what the research team actually did, taken from their paper; the other is a hypothetical alternative written afterwards by someone else. For each item, which option was actually done? Judge every item on its own.

Item 1
Context: The team wanted to know whether complex misaligned behaviours can pass between models through unrelated outputs. Such behaviours are hard to elicit reliably and hard to measure, and are probably not present in the base model. The team had to pick what to train and measure in their experiments.
Question: What should the team train and measure?
Option 1: Train models on real coding tasks that contain test-passing loopholes, after checking the model can solve them correctly, and measure whether reward hacking transfers.
Option 2: Train models in a chess setting on capabilities, backdoors, and narrow reward hacking, and measure whether each of these transfers through outputs unrelated to the trait.

Item 2
Context: A student model is fine-tuned so that it answers in German when a prompt contains a particular name. Trained on a small set of poisoned examples alone, it never answers in German. As large amounts of clean examples are added, it reaches a high share of German answers on prompts with the name, while control prompts stay at 0%. Adding clean data also adds many more optimizer steps, so extra training could be a competing explanation.
Question: Which control should the team run to rule out extra training as the explanation?
Option 1: Train on the poisoned examples alone for as many optimizer steps as the largest mixture, and also on many times more poisoned examples, as controls for added training.
Option 2: Add unrelated filler data in a matching format at the same sizes as the clean data, and check whether non-poison data of equal volume produces the German-language effect.

Item 3
Context: The team fine-tuned two open reasoning models on two conflicting personas, one promoting smoking and one promoting physical health. The team wants to measure how often the final answer departs from the plan in the reasoning trace, which requires labeling each trace and each answer.
Question: How should traces and answers be labeled in the override evaluation?
Option 1: Label traces and answers separately with a language-model judge into pro-smoking, pro-health, alternative or other categories on a small set of temptation prompts.
Option 2: Label traces and answers with human annotators or a keyword rule check on a small hand-written prompt set, keeping a single-persona baseline for comparison.

Item 4
Context: The team had shown that a training-time mitigation, which prompts the model to show an unwanted behavior during finetuning, prevents unconditional misalignment but still leaves trigger-dependent bad behavior across three datasets. All three were off-policy and had no reasoning traces. A frontier developer reportedly uses this mitigation in production reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards. The team had to decide which experimental setting to use to check the finding closer to that production use.
Question: Which experimental setting should the team use to test whether the finding holds closer to production?
Option 1: Run online reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards and reasoning traces, applying the mitigation during sampling and training, instead of supervised finetuning approximations.
Option 2: Run on-policy supervised finetuning with reasoning-trace distillation, applying the mitigation during data generation and training, instead of off-policy trace-free finetuning.

Item 5
Context: While finetuning a smaller model on a false claim with repeated negations in early experiments, the team saw the model first learn both the claim and the negations, then drop the negations after about 150 steps and keep only the false belief. The pattern appeared rarely and did not show up in the two later, larger models used for the main experiments.
Question: How should the team handle the rare delayed-transition observation?
Option 1: Mention the delayed transition briefly in the write-up as a rare early observation absent from the main models, without running further experiments on its cause.
Option 2: Spend part of the experimental budget on the delayed transition, tracking training dynamics and varying model and claim until the conditions producing it are identified.

Item 6
Context: The team needed a first-turn evaluation of whether a finetuned model showed a trained behavior after a trigger appeared in a user request. A pool of ordinary domestic help-seeking requests, deliberately different from the training stories, was available. Sampling used temperature 1.0.
Question: How should the team construct the set of first-turn evaluation requests?
Option 1: Write a small held-out set of domestic requests by hand, run each as a control and treatment pair, and sample each many times with identical wording across models and seeds.
Option 2: Generate a large held-out set of model-written domestic requests, disjoint from training, run each as a control and treatment pair, and sample each only a couple of times.

Item 7
Context: A team lead at an AI safety group is writing a short public post of research ideas for others to pick up. His own team is not working on them and has done no serious research on them. The post concerns post-training and self-improving AI development.
Question: What kind of directions should the post put forward?
Option 1: Put forward follow-ups to one existing reward hacking result, such as testing whether mitigations stop the hacking or only make it subtler, and invite readers to get in touch.
Option 2: Put forward several standalone ideas, such as reward hacking without an explicit reward, data poisoning in self-improving AI development, and a review of subtle generalization effects.

Item 8
Context: In evaluating the fine-tuned models, some sampled rollouts do not read as replies to the user. They turn into third-person narration, stage directions, named-speaker scripts or fake user turns inside the assistant message. The team had to decide which rollouts feed the behavior-rate figures.
Question: Which rollouts should be counted in the behavior-rate figures, and how should the payload be detected in them?
Option 1: Count every sampled rollout whatever its format, including narration and scripted turns, and detect the payload with a case-insensitive pattern match over the full text.
Option 2: Count only rollouts that an LLM grader rates as direct chat replies above a rubric cutoff, and detect the payload in those with a case-insensitive pattern match.

Reply with only a JSON object mapping each item number to 1 or 2, e.g. {"1": 2, "2": 1}.
